# R3 Digest — Ark / Judgeship / Transition (5425–6650)

Source: David Toshio Tsumura, *The First Book of Samuel* (NICOT), commentary on 1 Sam 4:1–8:22.  
Slice: `.cache/tsumura-1sam-reingest-2026-07-18/slices/R3_ark_judge_trans_5425-6650.txt`  
All claims attributed to **Tsumura**; no outside fill.

---

### C-R3-01 | Ark narrative: YHWH not vanquished though ark captured
- **Claim**: Tsumura opens the Ark of God section (4:1–7:1) by stating that even though Israel was defeated and the ark captured, Yahweh was not vanquished; he remained Lord even in enemy territory.
- **Quote**: "Even though the ark was captured, Yahweh was not vanquished. He was certainly the Lord even in the enemy territory."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 1–5; NICOT p. 184–185 (section B heading and intro)
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[philistines]], [[divine-providence]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-02 | Independent “Ark Narrative” hypothesis questioned
- **Claim**: Against Rost’s independent “Ark Narrative” linking 1 Sam 4–6 with 2 Sam 6, Tsumura (with Miller–Roberts) argues that if an independent ark story existed it probably included Eli-house corruption in ch. 2 but not 2 Sam 6; different place-names (Kiriath-jearim vs Baalah of Judah) and later perspective make a single original Ark Narrative hard to prove.
- **Quote**: "Therefore, it is difficult to prove that there existed an independent 'Ark Narrative' as an originally single story."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 6–8; NICOT p. 185
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-03 | 4:1a as transitional link; Samuel not yet judge
- **Claim**: 4:1a is a transitional SETTING (A/aB type) linking ch. 3 to ch. 4; by then all Israel knew Samuel as prophet, but he had not yet assumed judgeship (first at 7:6); Eli still judged; the people went to war without seeking the Lord’s will through his prophet.
- **Quote**: "the implication of this verse as a whole, therefore, would be: 'Though the word of Samuel was recognized throughout Israel, the people went out for battle without asking the will of the Lord through his prophet.'"
- **Locus**: slice ll. 12–16, 82–88; NICOT pp. 185–188
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[samuel]], [[shiloh]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-04 | Elders treat ark as instrument; “take” as key term
- **Claim**: After defeat (about 4,000 slain), elders of Israel take the initiative to bring the ark from Shiloh as a cultic means of salvation; the collocation “take + the ark” is a key phrase—Israel took it, Philistines took it, then took it back—conveying disrespectful instrumental use of the sacred object.
- **Quote**: "The collocation take + the ark is a key phrase in this ark narrative. … The narrator probably conveys that the people treated this sacred object without respect as an instrument through which victory might be attained."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 23–32, 80–81, 105–110; NICOT pp. 186–191
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[shiloh]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-05 | Ark as covenant repository, footstool, battle palladium
- **Claim**: Tsumura explains “ark of the covenant of the Lord” as repository for covenant tablets and as Yahweh’s footstool/podium with cherubim throne; the elders’ full title and military use rest on the ark as battle palladium (cf. Num 10; Josh), a persistent idea that victory is inevitable if the ark is present—which this story does not fully dispel.
- **Quote**: "That the ark would inevitably grant victory is a persistent idea which even the present story has not been able to dispel."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 111–118; NICOT pp. 191–192
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-06 | Ambiguous “he/it may come”; trust in object not YHWH
- **Claim**: The subject of “come” (4:3) is purposely ambiguous; Tsumura prefers “it,” arguing the elders put trust in the cultic object rather than Yahweh himself, possibly magically.
- **Quote**: "However, 'it' is preferable, for it was seemingly the cultic object, not Yahweh himself, that they put their trust in"
- **Locus**: slice ll. 120–120; NICOT p. 192
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-07 | Full title “Lord of Hosts who sits on the cherubim” used ironically
- **Claim**: The full title for Yahweh as sovereign King of the universe ironically hints at the people’s confidence in the ark rather than in Yahweh whom the ark symbolizes.
- **Quote**: "with this full title, the narrator ironically hints at the people’s confidence in the ark rather than in Yahweh whom the ark symbolizes"
- **Locus**: slice ll. 124–125; NICOT p. 192
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-08 | McCarter on ark narrative theology; Tsumura’s framing
- **Claim**: Tsumura reports McCarter’s view that the ark narrative’s theological purpose addresses how Philistines could defy Yahweh and prevail: the narrative affirms Yahweh controlled events from the beginning; the ark was captured because Yahweh abandoned Israel on account of the Elides’ wickedness.
- **Quote**: "McCarter holds that 'the theological purpose of the ark narrative as a whole' is to deal with the problem of 'How can the Philistines have defied the power of Yahweh and prevailed?' The narrative affirms that 'Yahweh was in control of the events from the beginning …. The ark was captured because Yahweh had chosen to abandon Israel on account of the wickedness of the Elides.'"
- **Locus**: slice ll. 80–80; NICOT p. 187
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[philistines]], [[divine-providence]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-09 | Second defeat; ark captured; Hophni and Phinehas die as sign
- **Claim**: Philistines fight courageously; Israel loses ~30,000 infantry; ark is captured (lit. “taken”); Hophni and Phinehas die, fulfilling the sign of 2:34 for impeachment of Eli’s house—first experience diametrically opposite the Exodus.
- **Quote**: "It was totally unthinkable for the covenant people that the ark of the Lord be captured … This was certainly the first experience in the history of God’s people that was diametrically opposite the glorious Exodus experience."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 70–78, 150–156; NICOT pp. 187, 195
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[philistines]], [[shiloh]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-10 | Eli’s death over the ark; forty years judgeship
- **Claim**: Eli (98, blind, heavy) dies when the messenger names the ark’s capture—his concern for the ark exceeds even sons’ deaths; he had judged Israel forty years; šāpaṭ means “to rule” as well as “to judge.”
- **Quote**: "It is the ark that Eli is concerned about (as in v. 13), more than the defeat of Israel or even the death of his sons. … He had judged Israel for forty years."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 161–228 (esp. 191–228); NICOT pp. 195–199
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[shiloh]], [[samuel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-11 | Ichabod: “Glory was exiled”; contrast with Hannah’s naming
- **Claim**: Phinehas’s wife names the boy Ichabod (’î-kābôd, “Where is Glory?”), saying “Glory was exiled from Israel!”; gālāh means exile (not mere departure); Tsumura contrasts despair-naming with Hannah’s hope-naming of Samuel, and notes that contrary to her judgment Yahweh will demonstrate glory in Philistia.
- **Quote**: "But, contrary to her judgment (i.e., 'Glory is gone'), Yahweh is going to demonstrate his glory in the land of Philistia, as seen in the following chapters."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 229–270; NICOT pp. 199–201
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[samuel]], [[divine-providence]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-12 | YHWH’s sovereignty in Dagon’s temple; ark costly trophy
- **Claim**: Philistines set the ark in Dagon’s temple to signal Dagon’s conquest of Yahweh; overnight Dagon falls prostrate in adoration, then is mutilated (head and palms cut off). Tsumura’s theological summary: Yahweh’s sovereignty extends even to Dagon’s temple; though the ark was captured, Yahweh was not vanquished; God removed the ark from Shiloh and displayed power outside Israel (as once in Egypt) to teach he cannot be used.
- **Quote**: "Who controls history? This story asserts that Yahweh’s sovereignty extends even to the temple of Dagon. Certainly, even though the ark was captured, Yahweh was not vanquished. The Lord God himself had brought about the events, removing the ark from Shiloh and displaying his power outside Israel as he had once before in Egypt to teach the Israelites he could not be used."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 272–276, 292–309; NICOT pp. 201–203
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[philistines]], [[divine-providence]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-13 | Dagon: identity, etymology, Philistine adoption
- **Claim**: Dagon is the Canaanite/West Semitic Dagan (Ebla, Mari, Emar, Ugarit as Baal’s father); folk etymology “fish” (Rashi, Kimchi) rejected; grain (*dagan) connection secondary; Philistines (non-Semitic) adopted Dagon after arrival; biblical writers treat him as Philistines’ national god (Judg 16:23; 1 Chr 10:10).
- **Quote**: "Biblical writers clearly consider Dagon as the Philistines’ national god, however (Judg. 16:23; 1 Chr. 10:10)."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 328–331; NICOT pp. 204–205
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[philistines]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-14 | Dagon’s severed palms vs Yahweh’s oppressive hand
- **Claim**: Cutting off Dagon’s head and palms results from defeat in war; Tsumura notes the contrast of “powerless severed palms of Dagon” with Yahweh’s “oppressive hand” in 5:6–12; threshold custom of Dagon’s priests is “perhaps as much satirical as aetiological” (citing R. P. Gordon).
- **Quote**: "These 'powerless severed palms of Dagon' might be contrasted with Yahweh’s 'oppressive hand' in 5:6–12."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 334–340; NICOT pp. 205–206
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[philistines]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-15 | Tumors terminology: ‘ŏpālîm / ṭeḥōrîm; hand of the Lord
- **Claim**: “Hand of the Lord was heavy” (yad YHWH) recalls Exodus plague idiom; swellings (‘ŏpālîm, Ketib) are euphemistic “hill-shaped” growths that became taboo; MT Qere introduces ṭeḥōrîm “tumors” as clarification, not euphemism; collocation with mice has led most to identify bubonic plague, but Tsumura stresses MT credits afflictions solely to Yahweh, not mice as causal agents.
- **Quote**: "the narrator of the present account is not suggesting any causal relationship between the mice and the misery of the Philistines, for he credits the afflictions of Israel’s enemies solely to Yahweh."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 345–396; NICOT pp. 206–209
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[philistines]], [[divine-providence]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-16 | Ark’s “victory tour” through Philistia (Ashdod–Gath–Ekron)
- **Claim**: Panic and tumors follow the ark from Ashdod to Gath to Ekron; Tsumura (with R. P. Gordon) reads the movement as a parody of a victory tour with roles reversed—triumphant march of Yahweh’s ark through enemy territory.
- **Quote**: "As the ark moves on to Gath and then to Ekron (v. 10), the story begins to read like a parody of a victory tour, in which the roles of victor and vanquished are reversed. This is certainly a triumphant march of the ark of Yahweh through enemy territory from one city to another."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 383–408; NICOT pp. 209–211
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[philistines]], [[divine-providence]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-17 | Seven months; ’āšām compensation; five golden objects (mice = tumors)
- **Claim**: Ark stays seven months (maximum suffering); priests/diviners require ’āšām compensation—five golden swellings, “namely” five golden mice (waw explicative, not “and”); Tsumura argues only five golden objects, mice representing tumors by sympathetic shape/magic, not a second plague; golden value as tribute to offended god.
- **Quote**: "If we recognize that use here and in v. 5, 11, 18, all the problems disappear. … As far as the MT is concerned, the text never mentions 'mice' as a plague; the 'mice' were an offering to the deity."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 413–535; NICOT pp. 211–217
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[philistines]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-18 | Exodus allusions; harden hearts; cart and milch cows test
- **Claim**: Philistine priests warn against hardening hearts as Egypt/Pharaoh; root *kbd plays across heavy hand, lighten hand, and tribute (kābôd); new cart and unyoked milch cows (calves driven away) test whether Yahweh or “accident” caused disaster—only superior power would send cows toward Beth-shemesh against maternal instinct.
- **Quote**: "'only a strong impulse from a superior power' would send them off away from home toward Beth-shemesh. 'If that happened the Philisitines’ miseries could confidently be attributed to the Israelites’ God.'"
- **Locus**: slice ll. 465–547; NICOT pp. 212–218
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[philistines]], [[divine-providence]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-19 | Return to Beth-shemesh; Levites; list of five cities’ tumors
- **Claim**: Cows go straight to Beth-shemesh; burnt offering; Tsumura defends Levites in 6:15 as original (not secondary scribal insertion) given continued priestly tradition; vv. 17–18a list five golden tumors for Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, Ekron—“namely” five golden mice for city-plus-environs units (merismus: walled forts and surrounding villages).
- **Quote**: "So, in this narrative five gold mice, which stand for tumors, were sent by the Philistines to Israel as a compensation and a tribute. The compensation was made not just for the cities proper, but for the cities and their environs, that is, for the whole land of the Philistines."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 550–655; NICOT pp. 219–224
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[philistines]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-20 | Smite at Beth-shemesh; “great platform of Abel”; Kiriath-jearim
- **Claim**: Yahweh (or ark as direct agent, Lord as real agent) smites men of Beth-shemesh for looking into the ark—seventy men, “every five people out of a thousand” (Tsumura’s reading of MT); people acknowledge “this holy God” in a taboo-ish popular sense; ark sent to Kiriath-jearim, house of Abinadab, Eleazar consecrated to keep it—yet people’s relationship with the Lord remains unchanged for twenty years.
- **Quote**: "Even though the ark is safely back in Israel and a priesthood is provided to 'keep' it, the people’s relationship with the Lord remains unchanged. They are not giving due respect to their covenant Lord but instead have worshipped foreign gods and goddesses for twenty years (see 7:2ff.)."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 656–713; NICOT pp. 225–229
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[shiloh]], [[samuel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-21 | Structural place of ch. 7: terminus of Samuel’s story
- **Claim**: Against McCarter (ch. 7 as climax/preparation for kingship demand) and those stressing continuity into ch. 8, Tsumura argues from discourse grammar that 7:2–17 is a terminal literary unit of the “Story of Samuel” (chs. 1–7); vv. 13–17 move toward TERMINUS (“all the days of Samuel/his life”); ch. 8 is independent transition to Saul’s story.
- **Quote**: "from a literary and discourse grammar point of view, ch. 7 seems to be a terminal literary unit. … Chapter 8 is an independent chapter which functions as a transition to the story of Saul (chs. 9ff.)."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 721–730; NICOT pp. 229–230
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[samuel]], [[monarchy-request]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-22 | Twenty years; repentance at Samuel’s command
- **Claim**: After ~20 years with ark at Kiriath-jearim, all house of Israel lament after the Lord; Samuel reappears (absent since 4:1) commanding return with whole heart: put away foreign gods/goddesses, fix heart on the Lord, serve him alone for deliverance from Philistines; Israel puts away Baals and Astartes and serves the Lord alone—completing the judges cycle of apostasy–oppression–repentance–deliverance.
- **Quote**: "At last Samuel appears! The last mention of him was in 4:1. … But now the time is ripe for God, the Lord of history, to bring him back to the main stage."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 732–768; NICOT pp. 230–232
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[samuel]], [[philistines]], [[divine-providence]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-23 | Mizpah assembly; water pouring; Samuel first judged
- **Claim**: Samuel gathers all Israel at Mizpah (Tel en-Naṣbeh), prays, water is poured before the Lord with fasting and confession “We have sinned”; Tsumura reads the water as penitential (not primarily rain-charm), and records first explicit mention of Samuel judging (though primarily prophet).
- **Quote**: "For the first time Samuel’s activity as a judge is mentioned (see v. 15), though he was primarily the prophet of the Lord (see 3:20) and his word had authority all over Israel (4:1)."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 770–825; NICOT pp. 232–235
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[samuel]], [[philistines]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-24 | YHWH thunders; Philistines confused; stone Ezer
- **Claim**: Unlike later elders requesting a king, people ask Samuel to cry to the Lord for salvation; Samuel offers wholly burnt suckling lamb and intercedes; Lord thunders, confuses Philistines (storm-theophany language not necessarily Baal-myth derivation); Israel pursues to Beth-car; Samuel sets stone Ezer between Mizpah and Jeshen—“Up to this point/time the Lord helped us!” (spatial and temporal).
- **Quote**: "Unlike the later elders of Israel who request a king (ch. 8), the sons of Israel here ask Samuel to pray that the Lord may save them from the hand of the Philistines. … 'Up to this point/time the Lord helped us!'"
- **Locus**: slice ll. 790–861; NICOT pp. 235–238
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[samuel]], [[philistines]], [[divine-providence]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-25 | Philistine subjugation; peace with Amorites; idealized theocracy
- **Claim**: Philistines subdued; hand of the Lord on them all Samuel’s days; places recovered from Ekron and Gath; peace with Amorites—internal and external security. Tsumura reports McCarter and R. P. Gordon: idealized domestic stability demonstrates sufficiency of the old theocratic order about to be questioned (omitting later Philistine garrisons and Saul-era confrontations).
- **Quote**: "The somewhat idealized picture of domestic stability and of territorial integrity is manifestly intended to demonstrate the sufficiency of the old theocratic order which is about to be called in question."

### C-R3-26 | Samuel’s circuit: Bethel, Gilgal, Mizpah; altar at Ramah
- **Claim**: Samuel judged all his life; yearly circuit Bethel–Gilgal–Mizpah from home Ramah (compared with Mari diviner Asqudum’s four-town circuit); built altar at Ramah, adding a sacred site and preparing setting for ch. 8 and Saul’s meeting.
- **Quote**: "Thus, the narrator summarizes Samuel’s era: Israel was secure and stable both externally and internally under the judgeship of Samuel, for the hand of the Lord was on the Philistines and there was peace between Israel and the Amorites."

### C-R3-27 | Ch. 8 as transitional section: literary and historical
- **Claim**: Tsumura’s structural argument places 1:1–7:17 as “Story of Samuel” (with embedded Ark story 4:1–7:1); 8:1–22 as “— transition to the monarchy —”; 9:1–15:35 as “Story of Saul.” Ch. 8 is among the most significant OT historical-book chapters, marking transition from judgeship to kingship by will of people and Lord; Samuel reluctant yet compelled becomes “kingmaker”; Lord providentially guides, “though somewhat negatively.”
- **Quote**: "Taking these observations into account, the literary structure of the earlier chapters of 1 Samuel is thus: 1:1–7:17 'Story of Samuel' with the embedded story of 'the Ark of God' (4:1–7:1); 8:1–22 — transition to the monarchy —; 9:1–15:35 'Story of Saul'."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 902–952; NICOT pp. 242–245
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[monarchy-request]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-28 | Monarchy request: sin vs providence tension (overview)
- **Claim**: People, seeing aged Samuel and corrupt sons, request a new institution rather than a new judge—desire for stability “like other nations,” partly Philistine/Ammonite military stimulus, but ch. 7 shows judgeship was adequate/ideal; McCarter: motivated by desire/covetousness not necessity. Tsumura: not merely socio-political—serious religious offense rejecting theocracy; yet the Lord still guides history providentially through the change.
- **Quote**: "Here, too, it is the Lord who providentially guides the history of his covenant people, though somewhat negatively. … this was not simply a request for a socio-political transformation; it was a serious religious offense against Israel’s sovereign God."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 908–926; NICOT pp. 242–244
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[monarchy-request]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[samuel]], [[divine-providence]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-29 | Samuel’s hereditary “experiment” with sons as judges
- **Claim**: Samuel appointed sons Joel and Abijah as judges in Beersheba—unusual because judgeship was not hereditary (contrast Gideon Judg 8:22–23; Eli’s sons never said to judge); R. P. Gordon: “little dynastic experiment”; breach of waiting for divine appointment; foreshadows problems of hereditary kingship; same verb *śym “appointed” used for king in v. 5.
- **Quote**: "This 'experiment' of Samuel’s was certainly a breach of the old practice of waiting for the divine appointment of a new judge and was possibly a cause of his family problems. It certainly foreshadows the problems of hereditary kingship in obviating divine choice."

- **Claim**: Sons did not walk in Samuel’s ways: unjust gain, bribes, perverted justice (mišpāṭ)—progressing to climax; when religious leaders pervert justice, society dies; names Joel/Abijah (“Yahu is God,” “My father is Yah”) ironic.

- **Claim**: All elders come to Ramah requesting a king to judge them “like all the (other) nations”; age and sons’ behavior are pretext; they want a new institution, not a new judge. Request would transfer sovereignty from congregation/assembly to the king—fundamental socio-political and religious change.
- **Quote**: "Rather, these facts were simply pretext for demanding a king like all the (other) nations. … the people here request a new institution instead of a new judge."

### C-R3-32 | melek vs nāgîd; human king as vice-regent
- **Claim**: People request a “king” (melek); God will give a nāgîd (9:16). Tsevat (reported by Tsumura): ngyd when bond/subordination to God is preeminent, mlk when origin/base of power lies in the people. Regardless of terms, biblical conception: human king is simply (vice-)regent/deputy of the heavenly King.

### C-R3-33 | Uniqueness forfeited: kingdom of priests vs nations
- **Claim**: “Like all the nations” (also v. 20; Deut 17:14) means exchanging unique glory as chosen people—“kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exod 19:6)—for status in the world’s eyes; throwing away special status to identify with nations of this world.
- **Quote**: "So, what they hoped to do was exactly to throw away their special status as the chosen people of God in order to identify themselves with the nations of this world."

### C-R3-34 | YHWH rejected as king; theocracy rejected
- **Claim**: Matter evil in Samuel’s eyes; Lord: “it is not you that they have rejected; but it is me they have rejected from ruling over them as a king!”—rejection of theocracy and of Yahweh who has been sovereign King forever (Lord of Hosts on cherubim; king even before the Flood, Ps 29:10), ruling also over Philistines. Continuity of apostasy from Exodus to this day (abandon me / serve other gods).
- **Quote**: "for it is not you that they have rejected; but it is me they have rejected from ruling over them as a king! … the people’s demand for a human king was the rejection of this eternal king."

### C-R3-35 | Concession not approval; legally declare mišpaṭ hammelek
- **Claim**: Lord’s “listen to the voice of the people” is negative permission/concession more than positive order; Samuel must legally declare (hā‘ēd tā‘îd wehiggadtā) the right/rule (mišpaṭ) of the king who will rule (yimlōk) over them—shift of emphasis from judging to ruling as king, bringing monarchical social structure.
- **Quote**: "This is not so much his positive order as his negative permission, or concession. … the change of title from 'judge' to 'king' in ancient Israel would bring a new social structure, the monarchy, in which a king fundamentally 'rules over' rather than 'judges' the people."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 1059–1076; NICOT pp. 251–253
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[monarchy-request]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[samuel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-36 | “Right of the king” as procedural manual (not Solomonic retrojection)
- **Claim**: 8:11–17 is procedural/manual discourse listing normal monarchical rights: take sons (chariot, cavalry, officers, farm labor, weapons), daughters (perfumers, cooks, bakers), best fields/vineyards/olives to officials, tithes of seed/vintage and small cattle, servants and best calves/donkeys, climax “you yourselves will become his servants.” Contemporary Canaanite monarchical reality, not necessarily Solomonic retrojection; v. 18 warns future oppression—cry out, Lord will not answer that day.
- **Quote**: "Thus, 1 Sam. 8:11–17 simply presents the 'right of the king' to the people who requested a king to rule over them … What it describes is the contemporary reality of the monarchical regime known to the people from the Canaanite examples. … There is no reason why the present passage could not have come from the time of Samuel."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 1077–1132, 1181–1186; NICOT pp. 253–260
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[monarchy-request]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-37 | Pro-/anti-monarchy sources overemphasized
- **Claim**: Against Wellhausen’s late anti-monarchic source theory, Tsumura notes recent scholarship (Crüsemann, Weinfeld) dating ideological struggle earlier; distinction between positive and negative attitudes has been overemphasized—differences reflect complicated attitudes of God and people toward human kingship, not necessarily different sources.
- **Quote**: "the distinction between the positive and the negative attitudes toward the monarchy has been somewhat overemphasized. … the differences are not necessarily an indicator of different sources but of different attitudes of both God and the people who were confronted with the idea of human kingship in ancient Israel."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 997–1006; NICOT pp. 247–248
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[monarchy-request]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-38 | People refuse; king as judge and warrior; Lord concedes
- **Claim**: People refuse Samuel’s warning: “No! But a king shall be over us! … like all the nations; our king shall judge us and go out before us and fight our battles”—three functions (status among nations; centralized judge; military leader). Lord fought his battle before (7:10); now they concern their own battles and visible human kingship—“beginning of new distrust.” Lord again: listen and make a king; Samuel sends men home—drama at point of tension.
- **Quote**: "The Lord fought his battle before (7:10), but now the people are concerned with their own battle! Instead of the Lord’s kingship, they look to the visible human kingship. This is the beginning of new distrust by the Israelites of their covenant God."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 1187–1223; NICOT pp. 260–261
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[monarchy-request]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[samuel]], [[divine-providence]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-39 | From real agent of the ark to real agent of history: YHWH independent of Israelite victory
- **Claim**: Across the ark section Tsumura stresses that after capture “the real agent in the story is the ark itself” under Yahweh’s hand; Dagon falls without human presence; plague and panic force return; Beth-shemesh is also struck—YHWH’s power operates independently of Israelite military success and even against Israel when holiness is violated.
- **Quote**: "From then on the real agent in the story is the ark itself. Both the Israelites and the Philistines were controlled by the ark. … Yahweh’s sovereignty extends even to the temple of Dagon."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 80–81, 272–276; NICOT pp. 187, 201
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[ark-of-the-covenant]], [[philistines]], [[divine-providence]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R3-40 | Senseless request after secure theocracy (bridge 7→8)
- **Claim**: Closing summary of ch. 7: under Samuel Israel was secure; yet next episode shows people “senselessly request a new institution of kingship, rather than a new judge, despite Samuel’s opposition”—setting the theological irony of ch. 8 against ch. 7’s ideal theocracy.
- **Quote**: "In the next episode, however, the readers will know, the people of Israel senselessly request a new institution of kingship, rather than a new judge, despite Samuel’s opposition."
- **Locus**: slice ll. 894–896; NICOT p. 241
- **Targets**: [[1-samuel]], [[samuel]], [[monarchy-request]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### Key monarchy-request claims (priority cluster)
- **C-R3-27**: Ch. 8 is **transitional** (not start of Saul story alone, not continuation of ch. 7)—discourse structure: Story of Samuel → transition → Story of Saul.
- **C-R3-28**: **Sin vs providence**: request is serious rejection of theocracy; Lord still guides history “somewhat negatively.”
- **C-R3-29–30**: Samuel’s non-hereditary breach and sons’ bribery as backdrop/pretext.
- **C-R3-31, C-R3-33, C-R3-38**: “**like all the nations**”—forfeit unique election; refuse warning; want visible warrior-king.
- **C-R3-32**: **melek** requested vs **nāgîd** God will give; king as heavenly King’s vice-regent.
- **C-R3-34–35**: “**It is me they have rejected** from ruling as king”; concession; declare **mišpaṭ hammelek**.
- **C-R3-36**: Rights of the king as contemporary procedural list; cry unanswered on that day.
- **C-R3-25, C-R3-40**: Ch. 7’s idealized **theocratic sufficiency** as negative preparation for the demand.

### Key ark / judgeship claims (priority cluster)
- YHWH not vanquished (C-R3-01, C-R3-12, C-R3-39); Dagon prostration/mutilation (C-R3-12–14); tumors terminology and mice-as-images not plague-cause (C-R3-15, C-R3-17); return and Ichabod (C-R3-11, C-R3-18–20); Samuel judge at Mizpah, thunder, Ezer, Philistine subjugation (C-R3-22–26).
